chapters.title: Chapter 4: From Raw Data to Usable Signal

lessons.title: Aligning Alt Data with NSE and BSE Trading Calendars and Market Data

body.text: A satellite does not observe a weekend. The stock market does not trade on one. Every alternative data pipeline eventually has to reconcile those two facts, and getting it slightly wrong is enough to quietly ruin a backtest.

children.text: This closing lesson of the chapter joins two ideas you already have, the point-in-time knowledge date from Lesson 2 and the clean features from Lesson 3, to a third: the market's own trading calendar. Getting this join wrong is one of the most common, least glamorous ways a promising alternative data signal quietly falls apart the moment it meets a real backtest.

body.caption: Alternative data runs on a continuous calendar, the market runs on a much shorter one

cells: Every day of the year, weekends and holidays included, since satellites pass overhead, apps get used, and e-way bills get generated regardless of whether the market is open
A daily alt data series is naturally longer than a daily trading series over the same period
Weekdays only, minus a published list of market holidays that NSE and BSE coordinate closely with each other
You can only act on new information at the next actual trading session, not simply the next calendar day

children.text: Muhurat Trading: The Exception That Proves the Rule

Just when you think 'the market is closed on Diwali' is a safe rule, Indian markets add a genuine exception: a short, symbolic Muhurat trading session held on Diwali evening for Laxmi Pujan, even though the day is otherwise a market holiday. A calendar table that simply flags every Diwali as 'market closed, no trading data' would miss this session entirely. This is exactly the kind of detail that separates a calendar built from a general assumption and a calendar actually verified against NSE and BSE's own published trading holiday list.

body.label: Muhurat trading
body.value: A special session on an otherwise market-closed Diwali
body.context: A reminder that trading calendars have real, culturally specific exceptions, and any calendar assumption should be checked against the exchanges' official published holiday and special session list, never hard-coded from memory.

children.text: From Knowledge Date to Earliest Actionable Trading Date

Lesson 2 established that the earliest you can use a data point is its knowledge date. This lesson adds a second constraint: the earliest you can actually trade on it is the next real NSE or BSE trading session at or after that knowledge date, which is not necessarily the very next calendar day.

body.code:
import pandas as pd

# Maintain trading_days as a verified, up-to-date table sourced
# directly from NSE/BSE's own published trading and holiday
# calendar, refreshed every year, never hard-coded from memory
# or assumed from a generic 'weekdays only' rule.
trading_days = pd.read_csv('nse_trading_days.csv', parse_dates=['date'])
trading_day_set = set(trading_days['date'])

def earliest_actionable_trading_date(knowledge_date: pd.Timestamp) -> pd.Timestamp:
    candidate = knowledge_date
    while candidate not in trading_day_set:
        candidate += pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    return candidate

# A data point known on a Saturday, followed by a Monday market
# holiday, correctly resolves to the next real trading day, not
# to Monday just because Monday is a weekday.
print(earliest_actionable_trading_date(pd.Timestamp('2024-10-12')))
body.caption: Never assume 'next weekday' equals 'next trading day.' Resolve against a verified, regularly refreshed exchange trading calendar.

body.title: A Weekend, Then a Holiday
body.scenario: A satellite-derived crop health reading's knowledge date, the date it was actually delivered to your desk, is Saturday. In this hypothetical year, the following Monday is an NSE and BSE trading holiday, and Tuesday is a normal trading day.
body.prompt: What is the earliest trading date on which this reading could actually be acted on, and what mistake would a naive 'next weekday' rule make here?
body.modelAnswer: The earliest actionable trading date is Tuesday. Saturday and Sunday are not trading days, and the following Monday, though a weekday, is a market holiday, so no trade could actually execute on any of those three days. A naive rule that simply skips weekends and assumes the next weekday is tradable would incorrectly treat Monday as actionable, one full trading day too early, which would misalign the backtest's assumed entry point with the earliest point a real trade could actually have been placed.

children.text: Handling Mixed Frequencies: Daily Alt Data With Monthly Aggregates

A feature built from a monthly release, such as an e-way bill or UPI summary, needs to be forward-filled across every trading day until the next release arrives, so your model has a value on every trading date. The discipline that keeps this correct is the same knowledge date rule from Lesson 2: the forward-filled value must stay at whatever was known as of each trading date, only updating on the trading day at or after the new release's own knowledge date, not on the calendar date the new period technically begins.

body.title: Final Alignment Checklist Before a Feature Goes Into a Signal
steps: Confirm every observation carries both a period date and a knowledge date, as covered in Lesson 2
Resolve every knowledge date to its earliest actionable trading date using a verified, current NSE and BSE trading calendar, not an assumed weekday rule
For monthly or otherwise lower-frequency data, forward-fill across trading days only up to the point a new release's knowledge date is reached
Spot-check calendar edge cases directly, such as a Muhurat trading session or a holiday that falls midweek, rather than trusting a generic calendar library by default
Confirm the final aligned series has exactly one value per trading day, no gaps and no duplicate trading dates, before it moves on to Chapter 5's signal construction

body.title: A note on settlement: T+1 and why the calendar still matters after the trade

children.text: Indian equity markets settle on a T+1 cycle, meaning a trade executed on one trading day settles on the next trading day, not the next calendar day. This matters less for the signal construction covered in this chapter and more for realistic execution and cost modelling later in a strategy's life, but it is the same trading-calendar discipline showing up again: 'the next day' in a market context almost always means the next trading day, never simply the next calendar day.

body.text: Calendar alignment is the least intellectually exciting topic in this entire course, and it is also one of the most common places a real strategy quietly loses its edge between a clean backtest and live trading. Treat your trading calendar table with the same seriousness you would treat the data itself, because a wrong calendar corrupts every single feature built on top of it.

The specific dates used in this lesson's exercises are hypothetical for teaching purposes, not real NSE or BSE holiday dates for any actual year. Always verify the current trading and holiday calendar directly from NSE and BSE's own official publications before building a production pipeline.

points: Alternative data runs on a continuous, every-day calendar, while NSE and BSE trade only on a coordinated set of weekdays minus published market holidays

Muhurat trading, a special short Diwali evening session on an otherwise market-closed day, is a reminder to verify calendar assumptions against the exchanges' own official publications rather than general rules

The earliest a data point can actually be traded on is the next real trading session at or after its knowledge date, not simply the next calendar weekday, since a weekday can still be a market holiday
Lower-frequency data, such as monthly e-way bill or UPI releases, must be forward-filled across trading days only up to the point a new release's own knowledge date is reached
A final alignment checklist, verified calendar, correct forward-fill discipline, and a spot-check for edge cases, should run before any feature reaches signal construction
India's T+1 settlement cycle is the same trading-calendar discipline appearing again downstream, in execution and cost modelling rather than in signal construction itself
